examples.question_text: Rationalise the denominator of $\dfrac{8}{\sqrt{6}}$, giving your answer in simplest form.
examples.solution_text:
Multiply numerator and denominator by $\sqrt{6}$; this multiplies the fraction by $1$.
$\begin{align*}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\dfrac{8}{\sqrt{6}}\\&=\dfrac{8}{\sqrt{6}}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{6}}\\&=\dfrac{8\sqrt{6}}{6}\\&=\dfrac{4\sqrt{6}}{3}\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: Rationalise the denominator of $\dfrac{6\sqrt{5}}{4\sqrt{3}}$, giving your answer in simplest form.
examples.solution_text:
Only the surd needs clearing; the coefficient $4$ is already rational.
$\begin{align*}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\dfrac{6\sqrt{5}}{4\sqrt{3}}\\&=\dfrac{6\sqrt{5}}{4\sqrt{3}}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}}\\&=\dfrac{6\sqrt{15}}{12}\\&=\dfrac{\sqrt{15}}{2}\end{align*}$

Use the surd law of division, then rationalise.
$\begin{align*}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\sqrt{\dfrac{11}{6}}\\&=\dfrac{\sqrt{11}}{\sqrt{6}}\\&=\dfrac{\sqrt{11}}{\sqrt{6}}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{\sqrt{6}}\\&=\dfrac{\sqrt{66}}{6}\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: Rationalise the denominator of $\dfrac{4-\sqrt{10}}{2\sqrt{5}}$, giving your answer in simplest form.
examples.solution_text:
Multiply every term in the numerator by $\sqrt{5}$.
$\begin{align*}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\dfrac{4-\sqrt{10}}{2\sqrt{5}}\\&=\dfrac{4-\sqrt{10}}{2\sqrt{5}}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{5}}\\&=\dfrac{4\sqrt{5}-\sqrt{50}}{10}\\&=\dfrac{4\sqrt{5}-5\sqrt{2}}{10}\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: Write $\dfrac{15\sqrt{14}}{5\sqrt{2}}$ in simplest form with a rational denominator.
examples.solution_text:
Divide the coefficients and radicands separately.
$\begin{align*}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}\dfrac{15\sqrt{14}}{5\sqrt{2}}\\&=\dfrac{15}{5}\sqrt{\dfrac{14}{2}}\\&=3\sqrt{7}\end{align*}$
The denominator is already rational after simplifying.

examples.question_text: By rationalising the denominator, show that $\dfrac{2t}{\sqrt{t}}=2\sqrt{t}$ for $t>0$.

examples.derivation: Multiplying numerator and denominator by sqrt(6) gives 8sqrt(6)/6. Cancelling the common factor 2 gives 4sqrt(6)/3.
Multiplying numerator and denominator by sqrt(3) gives 6sqrt(15)/(4×3) = 6sqrt(15)/12 = sqrt(15)/2.
The division law gives sqrt(11/6) = sqrt(11)/sqrt(6). Multiplying numerator and denominator by sqrt(6) gives sqrt(66)/6; 66 has no nontrivial square factor.
Multiplication by sqrt(5)/sqrt(5) gives (4sqrt(5)−sqrt(50))/10. Since sqrt(50) = 5sqrt(2), the result is (4sqrt(5)−5sqrt(2))/10, with no common rational factor to cancel.
Dividing coefficients and radicands gives (15/5)sqrt(14/2) = 3sqrt(7). Its implicit denominator is 1, so the requested rational denominator is achieved.
For t>0, sqrt(t) is nonzero. Multiplication by sqrt(t)/sqrt(t) gives 2t sqrt(t)/t. Cancelling the nonzero factor t establishes 2sqrt(t).
